summary: This RFC discusses problems of connecting personal computers to the ARPA Internet over low-speed links and possible solutions. It is a discussion paper that says none of its proposals are meant as standards. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC asks what to do about connecting a personal computer to the Internet over a slow telephone line, where a single typed character costs forty-one bytes of packet. It presents three candidate protocols. Two of them compress the traffic on the line by sending only the parts that changed. The third puts a gateway in the middle that runs the Internet protocols itself, so the line carries only a simple stream of data.

questions: how to connect personal computers to the internet in 1984
how to compress tcp ip headers on slow links
what problem did the thinwire protocol solve
subtitle: A 1984 discussion paper on getting a personal computer onto the Internet over a telephone line.

tldr.problem: A personal computer with a telephone modem had a 1200 baud line, and a single character typed into a remote login took a 41-byte TCP/IP packet. At that speed the line behaved like a 30 baud connection, and typing was unusable.
tldr.mechanism: The paper offers three designs. Two compress the packets on the line by sending only what changed since the previous packet. The third drops the Internet protocols from the line entirely and lets a gateway at the far end run them.
tldr.outcome: The document is explicitly a discussion paper: none of its proposals are intended as standards. It is Historic, and the RFC says it hoped a consensus would emerge from the discussion.

today: RFC 914 was published in September 1984 and is a Historic document. The RFC says of itself that it focuses discussion on the problems of low speed network interconnection with personal computers and possible methods of solution, and that none of the proposed solutions are intended as standards for the ARPA-Internet.

sections.title: The Problem: A Personal Computer on a Slow Line
sections.content:
As workstations and personal computers are connected to the Internet, many of the usual cost and speed trade-offs change. With substantial computing power available in the three to ten thousand dollar range, it is feasible to locate computers at their point of use, including in buildings, in homes and in other places remote from the existing high speed connections. Dedicated 56k baud lines are costly, have limited availability and have a long lead time for installation, and high speed local networks are not an applicable interconnection solution. These two facts ensure that readily available 1200 and 2400 baud telephone modems over dialed or leased telephone lines will be an important part of the interconnection scheme in the near future. The paper therefore considers a thin data path, that is one slower than 9600 baud.

The cost and flexibility of telephone modems is very attractive, but the low speed produces major problems. A minimum TCP/IP Telnet packet, carrying one character, is 41 bytes long, and at 1200 baud the transmission time for such a packet would be around 0.3 seconds, which is equivalent to using a 30 baud line for single character transmission. The paper assumes throughout that the transmission speed is limited only by the speed of the communication line and that the line acts as a synchronous link when calculating speed; in reality, with interrupt, computational and framing overhead, the times could be 10 to 50 percent worse.

In many cases local echo and line editing allow acceptable Telnet behaviour, but many applications will work only with character at a time transmission, and multiple data streams can be very useful for taking full advantage of the link between a personal computer and the Internet. Hence the proposal.
sections.plainLanguage: The arithmetic is what drives the paper. One typed character becomes a 41-byte packet, and a 1200 baud line takes about a third of a second to send it. That is like typing on a 30 baud line, which is too slow to use. The paper is about how to send less.

sections.title: Three Ways to Attack It
sections.content:
The paper lists three forms a solution can take. The first is a non-solution: one can learn to live with the slow communication, which might be a reasonable thing to do for background file transfer and one-time inquiries to time, date or quote-of-the-day servers. The second is to use TCP/IP but intercept the link level transmissions and apply compression algorithms, which provides a symmetrical structure on either side of the thinwire. The third is to build an asymmetrical gateway that takes some of the transport and network overhead away from both the serial link and the personal computer, with the object of making the computer do the local work and of making the interconnection with the extended network a benefit to the computer rather than a drain on it.

The first form has the advantage of simplicity and ease of implementation. The second, compression at link level, can be exploited in two ways. Thinwire I is a simple robust compressor which reduces the 41-byte minimum TCP/IP Telnet packets to a series of 17-byte update packets, improving the effective baud rate from 30 to 70 over a 1200 baud line for single character packets. Thinwire II uses a considerably more complex technique and takes advantage of the storage and processing power on either side of the thinwire link; it compresses packets from multiple TCP/IP connections from 41 bytes down to 13 bytes, giving an effective rate of 95 baud for single character packets.

The third form balances the characteristics of the personal computer, the communications line, the gateway and the Internet protocols. Instead of running full transport and internet layers on the computer, the computer and the gateway manage a single reliable stream, multiplexing data on that stream with control requests. Without the interneting and flow control structures travelling over the communications line on a per-packet basis, the data flow can be compressed a great deal. Since there is some switching overhead and a reliable link level protocol is needed on the serial line, the average effective baud rate would be in the 900 baud range.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three answers. Do nothing and accept the speed. Compress the packets on the line, keeping TCP and IP intact. Or take the Internet protocols off the line entirely and let a gateway run them, which the paper calls an asymmetrical gateway because the two ends then do different jobs.

sections.title: Thinwire I: Send Only What Changed
sections.content:
The simplest technique for compressing packets that have similar headers is for both the transmitting and receiving host to store the most recent packet and transmit just the changes from one packet to the next. The updated information is transmitted by sending a packet that includes the updated information along with a description of where the information should be placed. A series of descriptor-data blocks makes up the update packet. The descriptor consists of the offset from the last byte changed to the start of the data to be changed and a count of the number of data bytes to be substituted into the old template. The descriptor is one byte long with two four-bit fields, so offsets and counts of up to 15 bytes can be described. In the most pathological case the descriptor adds an extra byte for every 15 bytes, a six percent expansion.

Appendix A shows the technique in action with a TCP/IP Telnet connection: a first packet simulating the typing of the character "a", a second packet for the typing of "d", and the update packet that would actually be transmitted. Each Telnet packet is 41 bytes long and the typical update is 17 bytes.

The technique is a useful improvement over sending entire packets, and it is computationally simple. It suffers from two problems: the compression is modest, and if more than one class of packets is being handled, the assumption of common header information breaks down, causing the compression of each class to suffer.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends keep a copy of the last packet. When the next one is nearly the same, the sender sends only the bytes that differ, plus a short note saying where they go and how many there are. The note is one byte, so it can describe a change of up to fifteen bytes at a position up to fifteen bytes further on.

sections.title: Thinwire II: Match Templates and Know the Protocol
sections.content:
Both of the problems with Thinwire I suggest that a more computationally complex protocol may be appropriate, and any major improvement in data compression must depend on knowledge of the protocols being used. Thinwire II uses that knowledge for two things. First, the packets are sorted into classes: the packets from each TCP connection using the thinwire link would, because of their header similarities, make up a class of packets, and recognising these classes and sorting by them is called matching templates. Second, knowledge of the protocols is used to compress the updates: a bitfield indicating which fields in the header have changed, followed only by the changed fields, is much shorter than the general form of change notices. Simple arithmetic is allowed, so 32-bit fields can often be updated in 8 or 16 bits.

A typical transaction is described in Appendix B, with template matching based on the unchanging fields in each class of packet. A TCP/IP packet would match on the network type field, the version, the type of service, the protocol, and the source and destination address and port. The 41 bytes have been reduced to 13. An additional advantage is that multiple classes of packets can be transported across the same line without affecting the compression of each other, simply by matching and storing multiple templates.

The paper lists the implications of this design. Saving several templates, one for each TCP/IP connection, means a relatively large memory requirement, which the authors consider reasonable for current personal computers; the gateway must also keep tables for several connections at a time. The thinwire links are slow, much slower than normal disk access, so there is no reason why inactive templates cannot be swapped out to disk and retrieved when needed if memory is limited. There is state information in the connections: if the two sides get out of synchronisation with each other, data flow stops, so some method of error detection and recovery must be provided. To minimise that problem the protocol used on the serial line must be reliable, and there must also be periodic resynchronisation, for example every Nth packet transmitted in full. The asynchronous link is not, by its nature, a packet oriented system, so a packet structure has to be layered on the character at a time transfer, although if the protocol layer below thinwire, SLIP, can be trusted the formation of packets is a simple matter. Finally, Thinwire II will need to be enhanced for each new protocol it is called upon to service, and any packet type not recognised by the Thinwire connection will be transmitted in full. For maintaining full network service, the authors conclude that Thinwire II or a close variant seems to be the solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Thinwire II keeps one template per connection, working out which header fields stay the same and sending only the ones that changed, plus a bit saying which fields those were. The price is memory, one template per connection, and the need for the two ends to stay in step: if they lose synchronisation, nothing flows until they resynchronise.

sections.title: Thinwire III: A Gateway Doing the Work
sections.content:
When transmissions at the link level are not required and only the available services are desired, a solution based on Thinwire III may be appropriate. The key is a star network with a gateway in the centre, serving as the connection between a number of personal computers and the Internet. Rather than providing connections at the network or link level, Thinwire III assumes that there is a reliable serial link, SLIP or equivalent, beneath it, and that the workstation or personal computer has better things to do than manage TCP state tables and timeouts. It also assumes that the gateway supporting the Thinwire III connections is powerful enough to run many TCP connections and several SLIPs at the same time. The gateway fills in for the limitations of the communications line and the personal computer: it provides a gateway to the Internet, managing the transport and network functions and providing both reliable stream and datagram service.

In Thinwire III the gateway starts an interpreter for each SLIP connection from a personal computer. The gateway opens TCP, UDP and later TP4 connections at the request of the personal computer, and acting as its agent it manages the remote negotiations and the data flow to and from the computer. Multiple connections can be opened, with inline logical switches in the reliable data flow indicating which connection the data is destined for, and additional escaped sequences carry error and informational data between the two Thinwire III communicators.

The protocol is not symmetric. The gateway opens connections to the wider Internet as an agent for the personal computer, but it cannot open inbound connections to the personal computer, because the computer is perceived as a stub host. The personal computer may however passively open connections on the gateway to act as a server, and extended control sequences are specified to handle the multiple connection negotiation that this server ability entails.

The paper acknowledges that the protocol seems to ignore the problem of flow control, on the grounds that the processing on either side of the link will be much speedier than the link itself, and that buffering for the communication line and the user process blocking for it will provide most of the flow control. For the rare instances where that is not sufficient, there are control messages to delay the flow to a port or to all data flow. A tentative specification for Thinwire III is attached as Appendix C.
sections.plainLanguage: The third design stops pretending the line is a network. A gateway in the middle runs TCP and UDP on the computer's behalf, and the line carries a simple reliable stream with switches saying which conversation each piece of data belongs to. The computer never has to keep connection state or handle timeouts.

sections.title: Appendices and the Status of the Paper
sections.content:
The appendices carry the detail. Appendix A is an example of Thinwire I compression, showing two single character TCP/IP Telnet packets and the update packet that would be transmitted instead. Appendix B gives examples of Thinwire II compression, with the description of the field definitions depending on the contents of earlier fields. Appendix C is a tentative specification for Thinwire III: it uses the ASCII character "z" as an escape character, with the byte following it interpreted as a command, because z occurs rarely in text and control data streams and should pass easily through lower level protocols; the format of a request is "z" request code, request sequence number, arguments, request codes 0 to 31 change the default connection, codes 32 to 63 are reserved, and codes 64 to 127 are for stream server open requests.

Appendix D is the Serial Line Interface Protocol, given as an example of a reliable protocol for the serial line. Its philosophy is described as a mistrust of serial lines and a margin of laziness, with examples including how it recovers from errors and how it handles resequencing. The message format begins with a one byte Start of Header token, 11111111, followed by a four bit sequence number and a four bit acknowledgement number, then a five bit length field specifying the length of the data in the message, then a three bit field of flags: the first bit indicates that a receive error has occurred and the acknowledgement is really a repeat of the last acknowledged message, the second indicates a Synchronize Sequence Numbers message and the third a Start of Control Message. At the end of the message is an exclusive-or checksum. The maximum data length is 32 bytes, which limits the vulnerability of receiver timeout errors occurring because of a bit error in the length field.

The status of the document is set out at the top. It focuses discussion on the particular problems in the ARPA-Internet of low speed network interconnection with personal computers, and on possible methods of solution. None of the proposed solutions in the document are intended as standards for the ARPA-Internet; rather, it is hoped that a general consensus will emerge as to the appropriate solution to the problems, leading eventually to the adoption of standards.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendices hold the worked examples, the tentative specification for the gateway design, and a description of SLIP, the simple serial-line protocol the whole scheme depends on being able to trust. The document makes no claim to be a standard; it asks for a discussion.

viz.caption: WHAT THINWIRE II COSTS THE ENDS OF THE LINE

items.title: Memory for templates
items.text: One template per TCP/IP connection, and the gateway must keep tables for several connections at a time.

items.title: Swapping to disk
items.text: Inactive templates can be written to disk and read back, since the links are slower than disk access.

items.title: Staying in step
items.text: The two sides hold state, so if they lose synchronisation data flow stops until they recover.

items.title: Resynchronising
items.text: The serial protocol has to be reliable, and every Nth packet can be sent in full to resynchronise.

items.title: Packets over a stream
items.text: An asynchronous line carries characters, not packets, so a packet structure has to be layered on top.

items.title: New protocols
items.text: Each new protocol needs its own enhancement, and unrecognised packets are sent in full.
